# First Circuit Denies Cancellation of Removal Where Child's Asthma Was Treatable
The First Circuit has denied a petition for review filed by a Salvadoran father seeking cancellation of removal based on hardship to his two U.S. citizen children, one of whom suffers from asthma, holding that the immigration judge properly applied the BIA's hardship factors and that her underlying factual findings about the severity and treatability of the child's condition were unreviewable.
The Court held that it lacked jurisdiction to revisit the judge's factual findings that the son's asthma was under control and that the father failed to show he could not obtain or afford treatment in El Salvador, but retained jurisdiction to confirm the judge had not simply ignored the medical evidence. Because the judge expressly discussed the son's medications, hospitalizations, and the family's finances before concluding that the cumulative hardship fell short of the exceptional and extremely unusual standard, the Court found no legal error and denied the petition.
The full text of *Espinoza Benitez v. Blanche* can be found here: https://www.ca1.uscourts.gov/sites/ca1/files/opnfiles/25-2029P-01A.pdf

# Hardship claim based on asthma rejected
After an evidentiary hearing, an immigration judge held that the petitioner failed to meet his burden to establish exceptional and extremely unusual hardship, including that the petitioner failed to demonstrate that J.P.E.’s asthma constituted a serious medical condition or that, even if it did, he could not obtain medical treatment for J.P.E.’s condition in El Salvador.

That decision was upheld by a three-judge panel of the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.
“To the extent [the petitioner] challenges the IJ’s factual findings about J.P.E.’s asthma that supported her ultimate lack of hardship determination, we do not have jurisdiction to review those underlying factual findings. … And to the extent he contends that the IJ ignored relevant evidence about J.P.E.’s medical condition altogether, which is a legal claim that we have jurisdiction to review de novo, … we reject that claim.
The IJ expressly discussed J.P.E.’s asthma, the medications [the petitioner] needs to treat J.P.E.’s asthma, J.P.E.’s two visits to the hospital, and [the petitioner]’s concerns that he would be unable to obtain that medication at an affordable price in El Salvador and that [the petitioner] and J.P.E. would live about forty-five minutes from a hospital if they returned.
But the IJ concluded that the evidence presented on these issues was not enough to bring any hardship to the ‘exceptional and extremely unusual’ level required by the statute. The IJ did not overlook this evidence,” Lynch added.
The eight-page decision is *Espinoza Benitez v. Blanche, et al.*, Lawyers Weekly No. 01-200-26.

The First Circuit denied Carlos Rene Espinoza Benitez’s petition for review of the Board of Immigration Appeals’ decision affirming the Immigration Judge’s denial of cancellation of removal. The petitioner sought relief under 8 U.S.C. § 1229b(b)(1)(D), arguing that his deportation to El Salvador would cause “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” to his two U.S. citizen children, specifically citing the inability to afford asthma medication for his son. The court applied the standard of review established in *Wilkinson v. Garland*, 601 U.S. 209 (2024), which restricts jurisdiction to reviewing the agency’s application of the “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship” legal standard to a given set of facts, while barring review of underlying factual findings. Under this deferential standard, the court found that the Immigration Judge properly applied BIA precedent, including *Matter of Monreal-Aguinaga*, by weighing relevant factors in the aggregate. The court held that the IJ reasonably determined the petitioner failed to meet his burden because the evidence did not demonstrate that his son’s asthma constituted a serious medical condition requiring treatment unavailable in El Salvador, nor did it show that the family could not afford such treatment. Furthermore, the court rejected the argument that the case was analogous to *Matter of Gonzalez Recinas*, noting significant differences in family structure and language barriers. As a result of the denial, the petitioner’s request for cancellation of removal remains denied, and the order of removal stands.

jina.title: First Circuit Denies Cancellation of Removal Where Child's Asthma Was Treatable — Law Office of Sabrina Damast, Inc
jina.snippet:
The First Circuit has denied a petition for review filed by a Salvadoran father seeking cancellation of removal based on hardship to his two U.S. citizen children, one of whom suffers from asthma, holding that the immigration judge properly applied the BIA's hardship factors and that her underlying factual findings about the severity and treatability of the child's condition were unreviewable.

The Court held that it lacked jurisdiction to revisit the judge's factual findings that the son's asthma was under control and that the father failed to show he could not obtain or afford treatment in El Salvador, but retained jurisdiction to confirm the judge had not simply ignored the medical evidence. Because the judge expressly discussed the son's medications, hospitalizations, and the family's finances before concluding that the cumulative hardship fell short of the exceptional and extremely unusual standard, the Court found no legal error and denied the petition.

# Arbitration Clause Unenforceable Where Purchase Order Failed to Expressly Modify MSA 

# C lean Energy Services CES LLC petitioned to per-manently stay an ICC arbitration commenced by GE Vernova International LLC and General Elec-tric International Inc. concerning turbine replace-ment work at the Willow Creek Wind Farm. The parties operated under a Master Services Agree-ment that required disputes to proceed through litigation in specified New York courts, while a later purchase order incorporated terms of purchase containing an ICC arbitration clause. GE argued the purchase order and incorporated rules delegated arbitrability and required arbitration. The court held that the MSA controlled because it expressly provided that its terms prevail over conflicting purchase order provi-sions unless an order expressly stated the MSA was overridden or modified. The purchase order contained no such statement. Reasoning that contractual hierarchy, not assent to electronic terms, governed the forum dispute, the court found the arbitration and delegation provisions inapplicable. It therefore granted the petition, permanently stayed the ICC proceeding, barred further prosecution of that arbitration, and clarified that it decided only arbitrability.

Carlos Rene Espinoza Benitez v. Todd Blanche

September 1, 2026 · 25-2029 · Panel Decision · Lynch · By Raj Patel
The United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit denied a petition for review of a Board of Immigration Appeals order. The court upheld the Immigration Judge's finding that the petitioner failed to prove exceptional and extremely unusual hardship to his children.
Listen to this decision 0:00 / 1:10
Download
Report a problem with this audio

Key takeaways

* Holding: The First Circuit denied the petition for review, affirming the Immigration Judge's determination that the petitioner failed to meet the burden of proving exceptional and extremely unusual hardship to his qualifying relatives.
* Standard: exceptional and extremely unusual hardship standard
* Vote: Panel Decision
* Practical effect: The denial of the petition for review affirms the removal order against the petitioner, leaving him subject to deportation to El Salvador.

Background

Carlos Rene Espinoza Benitez, a native and citizen of El Salvador, sought cancellation of removal after being charged with removability for overstaying his visa. He argued that his removal would cause exceptional and extremely unusual hardship to his two United States citizen children, specifically his son who suffers from asthma. The Immigration Judge denied the application, finding the son’s condition was treatable and the petitioner failed to prove he could not afford or obtain medication in El Salvador. The Board of Immigration Appeals affirmed the decision without a separate opinion.

A recent First Circuit Court of Appeals decision underscores that legitimate workplace discipline, performance management, and personnel decisions may proceed *even after *an employee engages in protected activity. **Key Takeaways **

- Requesting reasonable accommodations or reporting alleged discriminatory treatment (i.e., engaging in protected activity) does not immunize an employee from legitimate workplace discipline—so long as that discipline is not a pretext for retaliation.

- Employers should develop a trial strategy early and tailor discovery requests to their defenses.

# ESPINOZA v. BLANCHE (2026)
## United States Court of Appeals, First Circuit.
###
Carlos Rene ESPINOZA Benitez, Petitioner, v. Todd BLANCHE, Attorney General, Respondent.*
### No. 25-2029
### Decided: September 01, 2026
### Before Rikelman, Lynch, and Aframe, Circuit Judges.
### Kristian R. Meyer, Kevin P. MacMurray, and MacMurray & Associates on brief for petitioner. Marie V. Robinson, Attorney, United States Department of Justice, Office of Immigration Litigation, Brett A. Shumate, Assistant Attorney General, Civil Division, and Cindy S. Ferrier, Assistant Director, Office of Immigration Litigation, on brief for respondent.
Carlos Rene Espinoza Benitez (“Espinoza”), a native and citizen of El Salvador, seeks review of the decision by the Board of Immigration Appeals (“BIA”) affirming the Immigration Judge's (“IJ”) denial of cancellation of removal. In 2018, after the Department of Homeland Security (“DHS”) started removal proceedings, Espinoza conceded removability and sought cancellation of removal on the grounds that it would result in “exceptional and extremely unusual hardship,” 8 U.S.C. § 1229b(b)(1)(D), to his two U.S. citizen children: his daughter, D.E., who was nineteen years old in 2020, and his son, J.P.E., who was then seventeen years old. Espinoza argued that, if removed to El Salvador, he would not be able to provide J.P.E. with his necessary asthma medication. He did not make a similar argument as to D.E.
The IJ, after an evidentiary hearing, held that Espinoza had failed to meet his burden to establish exceptional and extremely unusual hardship, including that Espinoza failed to demonstrate that J.P.E.’s asthma constituted a serious medical condition or that, even if it did, he could not obtain medical treatment for J.P.E.’s condition in El Salvador. We deny Espinoza's petition.

The petition for review is denied.
